note: Optional textures for the served copy. The single-file build has no assets folder and falls back to flat colour, so nothing here is required to play.
rule: Nothing generated may stand in for real map data. Everything left in here dresses the player, who has no real-world counterpart to fetch, so nothing invented is displacing anything measured.
generatedWith: Pixa (FLUX 2 Klein), prompted for seamless tileable material

kit.note: The character's own gear — drawn in every mode, because no provider on Earth publishes a photograph of your jacket.

model.note: Generated character mesh, TRELLIS.2 via Hugging Face. The baked ground plane is cut away and the holes it left in the boot soles are closed; everything else is exactly as the generator made it - a 1024-pixel PNG atlas and float32 positions, normals and texture coordinates. 3.9 MB to 2.7 MB, and the 1.2 MB of that saving is a metal-roughness map nothing reads. Off by default.
model.rocketNote: Generated firework, TRELLIS.2 from a reference image, clustered down by tools/glb-optimise.py and then repaired by tools/glb-heal.py. It shipped once with holes in it - 21.8% of its edges open against 0.3% for the character - because the clusterer keyed its weld on the texture coordinate as well as the cell, so two vertices at one place with different coordinates stayed two and every chart boundary tore. The clusterer is fixed for anything made from now on; this file was mended in place instead, because the thing that generates it is behind a daily quota: weld what should have been one vertex, then trace every boundary loop and close it with a fan, repeatedly, until a pass finds none. 21.8% open to 0.7%. The tool prints the share on every run and the self-test refuses anything here over one per cent. Off by default: the holes were the fault, but at the size it is actually seen the built rocket still reads better, because this one carries a photograph with its own lighting baked into it. Settings -> Player -> Scanned firework. It also carried a second picture, declared image/png, whose bytes are not a PNG - they are little-endian sixteen-bit numbers, a piece of geometry that ended up under an image entry - and it was in the file from the first commit that added it. Nothing caught it because nothing looked: no material named its texture, and three.js decodes an image only when a material asks for one. tools/glb-prune.py walks a file the way a renderer walks it and drops what is never reached, renumbering the rest and rebuilding the binary chunk from only the views still pointed at; every accessor reads back byte for byte identical and the file is 17 KB smaller. The self-test now asks of every picture in every mesh here that it begins the way the format it claims begins, and that some material actually wants it.
model.normalsNote: Both meshes shipped smudged black, and it was one fault in tools/glb-optimise.py rather than anything about the bake. glTF wants every vertex attribute aligned to four bytes, so three signed bytes of normal are written as four - correct, except the padding has to be declared as the bufferView's byteStride, and it was not. Undeclared means tightly packed, so every reader stepped three bytes at a time through data written four apart: the first normal right and each one after dragged a byte further out of place, mixing one vertex's z into the next one's x. Half of them arrived as directions of no particular length, and a short normal draws dark, which is why the smudges followed nothing you could see in the texture. The character's bytes were still all there, so declaring the stride recovered it exactly; the firework's were not, because tools/glb-heal.py had already read them the same wrong way and written the result down as floats, so its normals are recomputed from its own triangles instead. Both tools are fixed, tools/glb-normals.py does the repair, and the self-test now reads every mesh here the way a glTF reader reads it and refuses a single normal that is not unit length.
model.wingsNote: It was generated wearing a spread pair of feathered wings, and the game strapped an elytra on over the top of them - two pairs at once. Cutting the scan's off was tried and is in the history as a warning: every rule that took the feathers took a strip of sleeve with them or left a ruff across the shoulders that read as a backpack, and the weld needed to close the wound afterwards merged eight thousand vertices that shared a place but not a texture coordinate, which dragged the picture across the atlas at every chart boundary and covered a clean figure in cracks. They are better wings than the built sheet anyway. So they are kept and hinged: a joint each, folded on the same signal the built pair takes, and the built pair comes off while the scan is the body on screen.
model.riggedNote: It arrived as one fused surface with no skeleton, so it stood rigid while the built figure walked, and the firework hung in mid-air beside it - the hand a rocket is held in belongs to the built arm, and the scan's own hand had no reason to be near it. It is given a skeleton at load: the joints the built figure has, a shoulder and a hip each side, a neck, and one for each wing, laid out in exactly the numbers the built rig uses so the two are the same skeleton, with every vertex weighted to the four nearest so a shoulder bends instead of shearing. The shoulder needed a collarbone as well as a spine to hang off, or the arm claimed it and dragged the chest out with it. It was also on backwards from the day it was added - reconstructed facing +Z while the eyes, the toes and the shoulders of everything else in this project face -Z - so every photograph of it was the back of a head. And it was measured wrong: the wing tips reach higher than the crown, so scaling the bounding box to one unit made everybody an eighth shorter than the height they had set. The loader turns it, and measures the head.
model.faceNote: The generated head is a smooth egg - no eyes, no mouth, nothing on either side of it - and a head with no front is a figure whose facing you cannot read at any distance, which is why the built model has two blocks for eyes. Until the generator is free again it gets a drawn-on one: two eyes and a smile in the same dark the built model uses, sitting a couple of millimetres proud of the skull so the corners do not sink into it, hung off the head joint so they turn when the head turns. The self-test checks they are on the front, because facing backwards is the fault this asset arrived with.
model.qualityNote: It shipped soft for a fortnight and that was this pipeline, not the generator. tools/glb-optimise.py halved the 1024-pixel atlas to 512 and re-encoded it as JPEG to hold the file under a megabyte: three quarters of the picture, plus what JPEG does to every hard edge - the mush along the sleeve seams, the smeared boot, the flat face. That trade is right for an asset everybody downloads and wrong for one that is off by default and never in the single-file build. Passing a texture size of 0 now means leave the pictures and the numbers exactly as they are and only take the floor out, which is how this file is made.
model.shadowNote: The strip of sleeve under each folded wing came back from the generator with no light in it at all, because it only ever saw the figure from outside. Standing still nothing looks at them; in a glide the arms swing a hundred and forty degrees and both are pointed at the camera, which was the pair of black gashes across the shoulders. Not holes: the same mesh in the same pose rendered plain white has neither, and those triangles have the same texture-area-to-surface-area ratio as their neighbours, so they are looking exactly where they should. There is simply nothing there. tools/glb-repaint.py paints them from the lit texels of the same part of the same body, and three things had to be right before it could be aimed at them and nothing else. An absolute darkness threshold is useless on a dark garment - this jacket runs from luminance 26 to 64, so any number that catches a gash catches a third of the sleeve - so the threshold is a fraction of what the same square centimetre of body is painted like. The neighbourhood that compares against is five centimetres rather than two, because a gash is four across and a smaller one is measured against itself, and it is taken twice, the second time over only the texels the first pass did not call dark, or the colour a gash is repaired to is dragged down by the gash. And the box has a front and a back, because the one that covers the unlit shoulders also covers the pocket on the chest, and the pocket is dark because it is dark. 28,483 texels, all of them on the two shoulders, each taking 72 per cent of the lit sleeve nearest it - so it stays a crease and stops being a hole. The tool's mark mode paints what it would repaint in magenta instead, which is how the region was chosen: by rendering it and looking, not by reasoning about where the fault must be. It opens the atlas as it was stored rather than converting it to RGB, because this one is RGBA with a real alpha channel and converting threw that channel away - nothing on screen changed, the material is OPAQUE, but the shipped picture quietly stopped being the generator's picture. It is byte for byte the generator's now apart from the 28,405 texels this repairs, alpha included.
model.soleNote: Both boot soles came out wrong three times running, and each fix was aimed at the paint when the fault was in the shape. The ground cut takes the underside of both boots away with the floor, leaving one long concave outline per boot. A point in the middle of the hole needed a texture coordinate, the average of the rim was taken, and a hole's rim is not a neighbourhood in the atlas - smeared rainbow. A fan from a corner the hole already has invents no coordinate and is exact on a crack a few vertices long, but across a boot sole it lays skinny overlapping triangles on top of each other, some of them wound backwards - the pitted black mess. And flattening whatever triangle stretched furthest across the atlas caught the sole along with 169 triangles of thigh, hem, collar and shoulder, each one a real piece of the photograph replaced by a colour from somewhere else; that threshold was measured on an older cut, and the widest original triangle in this file reaches 1.9 times the median, not 300. tools/glb-fill.py ear-clips each outline in the plane it lies in, walked backwards so the patch faces the way the surface around it does, and gives the patch the normal of that plane rather than the rim's, which lean outward along the side of the boot. Colour is decided per hole, not per triangle: a rim inside one chart keeps its own coordinates and nothing is repainted, and a rim stitched from pieces across the atlas gives the whole hole one colour, from the single point on it that the rest of the rim is nearest to. Four holes in this mesh, all four of them soles, none of them on the body. There is no photograph of the underside of a boot; the generator only ever saw the floor there.

removed: There used to be a scenery group here — foliage.jpg and rock.jpg — for the generated world. That world is gone: nothing is drawn from invented map data any more, so the two textures had nothing left to dress and were deleted rather than left sitting in the download.
